records.title: Show HN: Get your coding agent off ~2019 JavaScript, onto modern web primitives
records.author: paulirish
records.storyText:
Browsers natively handle a lot of what used to take 50 lines of JS (or a dependency): `CSS.highlights` for text range highlighting without <span>s everywhere, `<dialog>` and showModal() give you backdrops and ideal focus management, `field-sizing` to auto-grow textareas as the user types.. (Something yesterday's ftrain post touched on [0])

Models know about some of these by name, but consistently won't default to using the platform-native solution and instead prefer the incumbent <div>+JS based pattern. We started an effort in Chrome to supplement coding agents with this key domain knowledge and we're shipping our 1.0 today, in collaboration with Firefox, MDN, and Edge.

200+ guides (~1.7MB) of curated, hand-crafted implementation best-practices from web experts, updated as the web evolves. (Open source, obv, so.. we'll welcome your bikeshedding ;) Readable versions here: [1]

I've spent the last 9 months obsessing over how to ship this as an agent skill + (Agentic RAG) CLI without blowing up your context window. (Or cedeing activation mechanics to MCP dynamic tool search). The skill description is minmaxed for activating on relevant frontend tasks. The RAG work I'm pretty proud of… originally a 500mb native stack down to a ~7MB pure-JS package, ~10ms search on your CPU.

We just introduced a deterministic 'legacy-scan' (trained on 30k github repos) to identify old 'n dusted patterns that your agent can modernize. (92% avg precision on held-out repos.)

People make a lot of claims about what coding agents are good/bad at. We wanted receipts, so we invested heavily in eval infra [2] to help us hill-climb, but also to identify when knowledge is common enough we can prune our guides. (Ofc, some of the things we thought AI didn't know turned out to be wrong :) We run codex/claude/agy against 200 tasks without the skill and then with.. In total ~1,700 playwright/AST-based assertions. Agents go from 55% pass unguided to 92% guided.

Try it out:

    DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest install
    DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate dialog modal"
    DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan ./src
If you spot something wrong or weird, give us a holler!

Longer write-up on the 1.0: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/modern-web-guidance-v1

records.title: Show HN: I created a library for correctly using SQLite in Go programs
records.author: sethops1
records.storyText:
Using SQLite in Go is deceptively easy. If you just import the popular github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3 as the database/sql driver implementation and start making queries, things will work great until you start hitting SQLITE_BUSY errors as traffic increases.

Then you go down the same path of many gophers before you, finding GitHub and forum posts providing conflicting information on best practices for pragma values and connection handling.

So I created https://github.com/cattlecloud/litesql

Which provides a nice abstraction, making it easy to accidentally do the right things when using SQLite in your Go program. In particular it pools connections for read transactions and isolates a dedicated write connection for writes. It also sets pragma values to much more reasonable defaults, like isolation levels, foreign keys, cache sizes, etc. On top it provides a nice abstraction for creating periodic snapshots with retention policies. There is also litesqltest for one-line test database creation in unit tests.

Hopefully you or your agents might find it useful.

Hi, here's a TUI we originally created for internal use. The goal is to be able to control multiple Claude Code sessions running in parallel while being able to review the changes and to understand the design choices the agents make.

The key design principles are:

- the programmer's attention is the bottleneck, so instead of cycling between sessions to find what's waiting for user input we use hooks to push work to the attention queue, i.e. let work come to you, not viceversa

- easy change, review and comment loop: [tuicr](https://tuicr.dev/}-inspired code reviews. Easy to add comments and send them to agents

- unobtrusive tooling: run on tmux sessions, connect to claude code via hooks, no complex dependencies

- quiz mode: answer design questions about the code to verify and reinforce your understanding of the changes

- keyboard-first navigation with vim keybindings

Comments, ideas and PRs all welcome!

records.author: kyleandruczk
records.storyText:
hi HN!

I built Mimzie, an agent neutral AI workspace inspired by the Claude Suite (Docs, Sheets, Slides) and Cowork.

It's a free desktop app that runs ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok in their native CLI harnesses. Think T3 Code or Conductor but for knowledge work. It's basically a GUI for managing knowledge work agents in various form factors. One of those form factors is Bots, akin to Grok Bot or Dots.

The original idea for mimzie was simple: I pay for Claude and ChatGPT, and a lot of my day-to-day work lives in .xlsx, .pptx and .docx files. Moreover, I was sick and tired of losing context between AI platforms. I didn't want to bet the house on one AI lab's product, be it the ChatGPT or the Claude Desktop app.

So I built an AI desktop app that was agent neutral.

The goal of mimzie is to bring the kind of agent workflows that devs have had with codex and claude code into the hands of everyone. And to have a friendly GUI to do it. I've found that the personal agents, hermes and openclaw, are intimidating to set up and confusing to the average non-technical person.

some of the core principles of mimzie:

- your file stays your file: edits are done locally and .docx, .pptx, .xlsx, and .md and synced to the cloud after - every change is reviewable: edits show up as tracked diffs that you accept or reject, at the smallest unit that makes sense (e.g. a sentence in .docx) - free, and no new subscription needed: bring whichever AI plan or plans you already have. You shouldn't have to pay twice for the same inference, and you SHOULD take advantage of the insane subsidization in the current ChatGPT and Claude plans. - Bots with any AI: I love the concept of grok bot, not so much its limited choice of models. I strongly believe that long-standing "ai teammates" should be agent neutral and in your control

Try mimzie out: it's a free beta at mimzie.com

it's early, lots of rough edges, but I've had the time of my life developing it.

I'd love to answer questions and hear any and all feedback.

records.title: Show HN: Yogurt – Free, private, open-source alternative to Granola
records.author: brownrout
records.storyText:
Hey HN, I’m Eric and I want to share an OSS project that I’ve been building in my free time. Yogurt is a free, MIT licensed desktop app that uses on-device AI models to transcribe, summarize, and chat with your meetings.

Similar to Granola, Yogurt runs in the background and does not join your calls. But unlike Granola, Yogurt is open-source, free to use, and private. Your meeting transcripts, call recordings, and summaries never leave your computer.

As small OSS models have gotten faster and more powerful, Yogurt seemed like a pretty obvious win for privacy and cost conscious folks. You do not need a frontier model to summarize meeting notes or answer questions about them. And if you want to make your notes available to a frontier model, you can just share it with Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. directly via Yogurt’s local MCP server. There’s no need to use a paid cloud service as a middleman.

I tried some of the most popular OSS note taking tools, and most were missing features like calendar integration, MCP server, etc. or required you to connect or create an account. And more than that, they didn’t feel polished enough for it to be something I actually wanted to use daily, and so I built Yogurt to scratch that itch. I spent a lot of time fine-tuning every UI interaction/animation and optimizing the model calls to get the most out of your hardware + make it snappy.

To support Windows/Mac/Linux, I decided to go with Electron. I use whisper.cpp for transcription and Apple’s on-device SpeechAnalyzer if your system supports it. For call summaries and questions, I use a local open weight LLM that automatically gets downloaded and set up based on what your hardware can handle without your cooling fans firing off like crazy (this part uses llama.cpp).

I’ve spent a lot of time working on details like echo detection/reduction, global/folder/local level search respectively, and auto-end recordings. Hope this is useful for any of you who have held out on using AI note tools for privacy or cost reasons, or for folks using cloud tools who want to switch to something free and open source that still feels great to use.

Would love to hear what you think about the onboarding and note taking experience :)

records.title: Show HN: Perch by mxRaven, a self-hosted mailbox and CLI in 1 file
records.author: ku5h
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I have been working on mxRaven: https://mxraven.com for the past couple of months, and it has been hard to explain the idea without actually showcasing a functional use case, hence I decided to build perch.

Perch is a single binary Go program that can serve IMAP + SMTP as a complete mailbox service and has an agent-friendly CLI to access and manage emails.

Note that perch is open source under the MIT-0 license but it requires mxRaven to handle the public edge. However, the CLI (the `perch mail` command) can be used against any generic IMAP or SMTP submission servers (which are not necessarily perch). You can try out perch without signing up for mxRaven at https://tryperch.mxraven.com and can sign up for a free account with monthly 1k inbound + 1k outbound emails without a card.

The agent-friendly CLI was not an afterthought, since LLMs have been trained heavily for utilizing POSIX-compatible shell tools for various benchmarks, I believe agents are unbelievably good when you give them tools in the language they understand: CLI.

Perch can run on an old workstation in your homelab behind CGNAT or firewalls as it pulls mail in real-time from mxRaven's notification stream over a websocket. It also doesn't need to run 24*7, it can come online atleast once a day to pull the emails from mxRaven. mxRaven will not retain emails that are older than 48 hours as per our privacy policy, and it will not serve them to the pull-based consumer beyond 24 hours.

The hardest part about self-hosting email is the public edge, which requires managing IP reputation, throttles and a convoluted set of authentication protocols (DKIM, SPF, DMARC, ARC etc.) and mxRaven handles that.

Note that we also made a Show HN post for mxRaven itself here: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50338055

tldr, for those who don't want to read that: think of mxRaven as the WAF + router for your emails, while your applications can sit on the driver's seat for the email highway.

records.title: Show HN: Pots – Open-source Grok Bot alternative, used by 6 startups for a month
records.author: Crokily
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Crokily. Pots is an AI coworker that lives in the chat your team already uses: Slack, Discord, Telegram, or any channel with a Chat SDK adapter. It is MIT-licensed and runs on a machine you give it, with the model you choose.

To be honest, the first time I used Grok Bot, its design really impressed me. Unlike OpenClaw before it, it was not just Claude Code connected to a chat app. It truly cared about how it works with people. It felt like a living AI assistant, and working with it was painless. That is the idea I kept learning from the whole time I built Pots: it is not an agent hooked up to a chat channel. It should be a coworker that feels alive and is comfortable to work with.

But Grok Bot is only Grok's bot. Which model you get depends on your X subscription, your data and your machine are all in the cloud, and most of all, it is a standalone app, and most of its features serve that app.

Pots is a bit different. In Sydney I have talked with quite a few founders. Grok Bot is good, and it helps them a lot with their personal tasks. But when I asked who had actually put Grok Bot into their company's work to make their startup team faster, nobody had. So I think Pots is in a different place from Grok Bot, and from most open-source Grok Bot alternatives: it grew out of what real startup teams need. Before I open-sourced it, 6 small startups I met at startup events had been using it with me for over a month.

Pots is built first for the channels startup teams already work in, not for an app of its own, so most of what it does serves the places where you actually work. The teams use Pots as a middle layer: a CEO talks ideas through with the team in chat, Pots listens, and then it builds a prototype that both sides can check. They use Pots for competitor research: because Pots runs inside their channels, it knows their product well. Not only the GitHub repo, but the team's daily discussions and what the team cares about. Pots has been listening quietly the whole time, so it knows the product with no setup at all. It also works well with each channel: it talks to people with the channel's own controls, like Slack and Discord buttons and cards, and when it hands over something complex, it deploys a page with its built-in server so everyone sees it in a better form.

So Pots is different from Grok Bot and from most open-source alternatives. It came out of what real startup teams need. Its channel features start from what each company's work needs, and it can join your real work setup with no setup and still do well, instead of being one more app that nobody uses and that is hard to start with. And it ran in real business for a while before I cleaned it up and open-sourced it.

The difference from Grok Bot is also exactly why I made Pots an open-source Grok Bot alternative. I have OpenAI and Claude subscriptions with plenty of quota, and my own servers, so I don't want an X subscription to limit me. I want to use whatever model I want and do whatever I want. I can even switch to an open model, and none of my data goes into anyone's pocket.

Try it (Node 24+, macOS, Linux or Windows): the easiest way is to ask your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) to read docs/for-agents.md in the repo and set up Pots for you. Or by hand: npm install -g pi-durable-bot, then pots init.

I'd love feedback, especially on how it decides when to act.

records.title: Show HN: NoDOM high performance WASM UI kit for DuckDB-WASM
records.author: osullivj
records.storyText:
NoDOM replaces Chrome's DOM, CSS & HTML rendering with a custom WASM engine designed for high performance and minimal latency in Modern Data Oriented C++ for a zero alloc zero copy render hotpath. The aim being to minimise tick-to-render latency. GUI layout and data declarative JSON are served via websocket after initial page load, or can be packaged in an HTML shell like the UK property demo. The layout JSON supports embedded Forth fragments for "glue" computation. NoDOM can also call out to JS both synch and async. NoDOM builds on top of Dear ImGui and ImPlot, and builds to wasm with emscripten, and win32 with MSVC 2022. NoDOM is closely integrated with DuckDB-WASM; any table can be rendered as a grid or chart. I designed NoDOM with financial market trading apps in mind, having seen quants and traders frustrated by slow Plotly charts. Ultimately NoDOM should make it possible to show users dynamically generated high performance dashboards.

records.title: Show HN: Obeya, a spatial canvas for directing coding agents
records.author: sadilek
records.storyText:
Yeah, I know, "not another AI GUI rolls eyes". So let me say upfront: This is not for you if you want to regularly review the code agents produce. But if you, like me, stopped writing code at the beginning of the year and for the most part stopped reading it a few months ago, you are my target audience, and I think there's a good chance you'll benefit from this.

I love directing agents to build stuff. But oh, can you get lost in parallel coding sessions. Just walls of text. Cycling through terminal windows. It feels like pair programming with multiple people at the same time. Then: Start a dev server, navigate to the place of interest, click around to test a new feature. It feels like I'm the QA department of my agents.

About 6 weeks ago, I reflected on this for a few days and came up with a better way. I'm sharing it because it works so well for me.

Main idea: I want to be the agents' engineering director. I sit in the conference room and talk to them. Give them tasks. They come back and show results to me. I lean back and watch and listen to demo videos (mostly) or read presentation docs (sometimes). I give feedback orally to have them iterate. Or I approve, and they carry the change to main.

The work is laid out as cards on a canvas. There is color to show state, so cards can stay put, and I can build a mental map. I mostly drive it via voice. New task: Just say it. Something off in the demo video: Hold the space bar and say it, as if you're pointing something out in a review meeting.

There is a coordinator in the background that sequences cards for you based on their dependencies. It also runs regular retrospectives and proposes cards to improve your setup.

There are many more aspects I could describe, but then this post would just be another wall of text, so instead, in the spirit of Obeya, I suggest you watch the video at the top of https://obeya.si. It gives an introduction to Obeya, and it's an example of a demo video. All demos of Obeya's own development get published at https://demos.obeya.si if you want more examples.

records.title: Show HN: Rystic – Stateful Local Simulators of Slack, GitHub and Linear
records.author: evan_whitehouse
records.storyText:
Hi HN, we're Zach and Evan, founders of Rystic (https://www.rystic.ai). As LLMs have progressed, producing code has become fast and cheap but verification has not. At my previous company I noticed that whenever I could test a service locally or in CI this bottleneck went away. If a service needed to use a shared sandbox or staging environment to run integration tests, verification was a huge pain. At Rystic we are taking that idea and applying it to every third-party service. We are trying to give developers a way to verify that their code works without calling real systems.

To do this, we build deterministic simulators of APIs like Slack, Stripe and S3. You can control these locally; set their state and inspect it. Our aim is to make these a controllable stand-in for the real service, much more so than any sandbox. For this we offer fault injection, latency injection and multiple actor support. So for example you can cancel a subscription mid-cycle as the customer in the billing portal, then check that your app handles the proration and removes access. In the Stripe sandbox someone has to click through the portal by hand.

We recreate these applications as Go binaries to make them performant. A single simulator can handle thousands of requests per second. You can even control whether they get rate limited or not depending on how realistic you want your test to be.

To make the simulators we construct a set of tests based on their docs, probe their API, gather traces then use that to reverse engineer the state transitions of the application. Then we iterate on this by running deterministic tests and actively trying to break it. Proving this state machine is the same as the original would be NP hard but we can still show that they are equivalent over several hundred multi-step workflows. To make sure that our version stays accurate we test every night to catch drift and repair it. Each simulator's fidelity card lists its score, which is how closely it matches the real API across those workflows, and we share the failing tests with customers: https://www.rystic.ai/simulators

It is frustrating to have these incredibly powerful tools for producing code but then be left with the annoying work of verifying that what is produced actually works. No one wants to spend their day finding API keys, setting up sandbox accounts and manually clicking through applications. We are trying to make a future where that does not happen, where you can move fast and not break things.

We would love for you to give it a try. Any feedback is very welcome.

Here's a quick video on using the Slack twin to run evals: https://youtu.be/qwin0LAeaeU

Install:

curl -fsSL https://www.rystic.ai/install.sh | sh

brew install rystic-inc/tap/rystic

or download a binary with checksums from https://github.com/Rystic-Inc/rystic/releases.

Free: the Slack, GitHub and Linear simulators. No card needed. Everything else is $90 a month, and code HACKERNEWS will get you a month free.

Current simulators: Stripe, Slack, GitHub, Kalshi, PayPal, Lob, Okta, Linear, Resend, Anthropic, Clerk, Dropbox, Gmail, Google Drive, Notion, S3, Shopify Storefront, Word.

Coming: OpenAI, ElevenLabs, NetSuite, QuickBooks, Square, Sentry, PostHog.

We are rapidly adding more to our catalog and if there are any that you would like to see added, please let us know in the comments.

records.author: djacksondev
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I built Whisperstream, a free and open-source dictation app for Windows.

You've seen a dozen of these, so what makes it different from all the other dictation apps?

- Local cleanup: We're the only free and open source solution on Windows with a finetuned cleanup model. Stream-1 Mini is a Qwen 0.6B finetune for removing filler and applying spoken corrections. Superwhisper is the only Windows app that offers this, is paid, and in our benchmark we outperform their S1 mini with 36% less failures. Benchmark: https://whisperstream.io/stream-1-mini-vs-s1-mini

- Agent Speak: Hear or read response summaries from Claude Code or Codex, and speak back directly. Expand to see the full response without switching contexts. The TTS uses Kokoro for highly realistic voices.

- Smart Dictionary: Most local dictation apps don't offer dictionary support when using their fine-tuned cleanup model. We trained it into our finetune and use phonetic matching so we only include similar words for boosting.

It's GPL-3.0, completely free and now has a Mac version too.

Github: https://github.com/lanreal-io/whisperstream/

records.title: Show HN: Thousand Suns, a nuclear war sandbox
records.author: gxd
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm the author of Thousand Suns (1KS). This has been my full-time project for the past six months and is now available as freeware for Windows, Linux and macOS (experimental) on itch.io.

It started as a game but slowly turned into a serious simulation as I educated myself on nuclear war. I'm a stay-at-home dad, previously a Big Tech software engineer, and not a nuclear war expert. But I spent an enormous amount of time learning about the subject from original and derived sources, such as the well-known site NUKEMAP.

It goes beyond existing free projects by simulating full conflicts on top of single detonations. The conflicts are “all out” and meant to be a demonstration of the power of present-day arsenals rather than a depiction of nuclear war escalation.

This was made with Godot/C# and I spent a good amount of time hand-optimizing the code... Not because it was needed, but because it was fun! I'm not using any external libraries with the exception of Godot itself. It was all custom-made and the nuclear calculations were derived from the amazing 1977 book "The Effects of Nuclear Weapons" by Glasstone and Dolan.

I decided to make it free because I think it's important to raise visibility on what is, perhaps, the most dangerous threat to our survival. Without minimizing the many other risks we face, it is the one way civilization as we know it could end tonight.

Feel free to ask any questions and I hope 1KS is useful for you!

records.author: belcairn
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

I built Editmamei, a local MCP server for Adobe Photoshop and GIMP.

I built it because I wanted to connect Claude to a powerful photo editor, since Claude can't generate images itself. Apparently I wasn't the only one, Adobe previewed their own local Photoshop MCP yesterday, announcing at Adobe MAX a private beta in early 2027.

Editmamei brings the AI agent of your choice into Photoshop and lets it do as much or as little of the editing as you want. It has tools to measure and inspect, apply filters, transform the image, insert other images and create objects, and it can use some of Photoshop's more advanced features like Select Subject and Sky Replacement.

The agent "sees" each edit with downscaled previews, layer trees, histogram calculations and other tools, so someone who has never used Photoshop can ask for a recommended edit, and a professional can hand Editmamei the specific directions for tedious actions and batch automation, keeping the finishing and favorite parts for themselves. Everything is done layer by layer in a fully editable PSD, just as a normal Photoshop user would work.

Photoshop has more features overall, but GIMP is just as capable for normal photo processing and design. The main difference is the Adobe-specific tools; GIMP doesn't have heal/clone or AI subject and sky selection. Photoshop runs on Windows and Mac; GIMP runs on Windows, Mac and Linux.

Source available: https://github.com/editmamei/editmamei

I'd love feedback, and suggestions for other editors this could support!

records.title: Show HN: Ember.js, Re-Born in Rust
records.author: drauschenbach
records.storyText:
7 years ago I began migrating all my back-ends to Rust. Front-ends, however, remained an issue.

As an Ember developer for 15 years, I've been a big fan of MVC, and keeping code out of templates. Ember's HTMLbars syntax has been the thing I've leaned on to keep my templates clean and maintainable, so that I could stay focused and organized.

But the JS/TS toolchains were always a point of friction. As I worked on new Rust back-ends, while maintaining old Ember front-ends, I dreamed of rewriting those Ember routes, controllers, models, and adapters in type-safe idiomatic Rust.

The Leptos creator Greg Johnston finally gave me a nudge to get something going.

So after 3 years of planning, and 4 months of execution, the Auric framework is ready for public eyes.

It's Ember.js, re-imagined in Rust (and not just an AI port). It stays faithful to Ember, HTMLbars, and Ember Data, while leveraging Leptos to realize all of the reactive concerns (which implies Trunk for WASM packaging, and full SSR support).

It's open source on GitLab at:

https://gitlab.com/megalithic-llc/auric-spa

The sample app is the Auric website itself, which contains demo pages for all of ember-bootstrap, ember-power-select, and ember-concurrency add-ons, re-imagined in pure idiomatic Rust, backed by Actix Web based SSR. Templates and components are at /src/templates/ and /src/components/, while their code-generated Leptos counterparts are at /src/generated/views/ and /src/generated/components/.

Templates are up to 7x smaller than the Leptos views derived from them, thanks to the timeless elegance of HTMLbars. That seems like an important data point, now that our coding assistants threaten to automate us out of love with our webapps, by turning them into something we no longer enjoy looking at.

The longer back-story was published to Medium a few days ago:

https://medium.com/@david_77274/ember-js-devs-welcome-to-the...

records.title: Show HN: Zeus – Claude Code for AI voice agents
records.author: kolchinski
records.storyText:
Hey, Alex here, I'm one of the founders. We've built phone agents for enterprise customers for two years and kept seeing the same failure: agents that mishear callers and then do something confidently wrong.

We're announcing two things in this launch. #1 is the stack: instead of one transcription model → one LLM → one TTS, most conversation turns runs through several transcription models and LLMs (a fast and a slow LLM in the same call, models switched per turn, audio sent straight to an LLM alongside transcripts). That gets us 99.4% on Big Bench Audio. That's the second-highest published score; the only model above us takes almost 9 seconds to start talking as far as we've measured, which doesn't work on a phone call. Eval set and transcripts are on Hugging Face - http://huggingface.co/datasets/kolchinski/bba-storm-eval

#2 is Zeus, an agent that configures our voice AI stack per use case and per conversation. We tried doing this with Claude Code and Codex and they were bad at it: they can't run simulated calls out of the box, don't do well with audio input and spotting problems in calls, and tend to blindly believe vendor marketing about which model is best vs actually trying the models. Zeus has evals on real calls, can simulate calls in hard situations, and listens to production calls to find problems, so it can check its own work the way a coding agent runs tests to make sure the code it wrote actually works.

Pricing is cost-plus (vendor prices + hosting + a 17–25% margin), no subscription. Zeus is free for now. You can try it with a free $10 credit.

Happy to answer questions.

records.title: Show HN: AI Code Rating – a 3 character disclosure of how AI was used in a repo
records.author: gregdotca
records.storyText:
Hello HN!

Have you ever wanted to quickly determine an open source project's AI use? Me too, so I've come up with a spec that I think may help solve the issue. Maybe it'll be useful, or maybe it'll be crap, you decide!

AI Code Rating - Three simple characters that tell a reader who maintains a project, how much of its code is written by AI, and how closely a human checks the AI's work.

That's it, that's the whole idea. Repo maintainers assign a rating and save it, along with a quick blurb about how AI was used in the project, in an ACR.md file in the root of their repo.

The rating doesn't judge, it simply answers some questions at a glance.

If this sounds at all interesting to you, I'd love to hear your feedback!

https://aicoderating.com

Example: DomainMOD, rated "B1b" (a project I wrote and have maintained since 2010)

B = "Experienced" - Works professionally in this stack. Could write the whole project unaided.

1 = "A little" - 1–25% of the code. AI wrote pieces such as tests, boilerplate, or single functions.

b = "Reviewed" - Every AI change read by a person before merge. Tests where practical.

Full Disclosure: The ACR website itself is rated B4b. AI wrote nearly all the code and text, directed by me, and I reviewed its work.

records.title: Show HN: EarthData – find places to visit or live that match what you care about
records.author: 11thEarlOfMar
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

A few years ago, I was trying to find the place on Earth that had the optimal combination of attributes to vacation to or live. I couldn't find anything that wasn't a marketing funnel or was limited in geography. So I built EarthData essentially for myself, but others might find it useful.

There are two modes: "visit" for a trip (travel month, length of stay, things to do) and "live" for relocation or retirement (housing, healthcare, day-to-day fit).

The way it operates is to allow the user to sculpt the attributes they care about in where they visit on vacation or live. Rate and rank what matters to you. And it will returns 10 initial places, down to specific towns, with a written explanation of why each one fits. From there, the user can expand on places that look interesting, and ultimately pull a TRIP KIT with full itinerary, web links to venues, packing list and other information.

A few design choices:

- It's anonymous. No account, no email required, and preferences live in your browser's local storage. Nothing is tied to a named profile, your preferences are sent to xAI's API to generate matches, but without any PII.

- No ads and no advertising cookies.

- I went with a mid-century travel graphic design. To me, it evokes nostalgia and romance for international travel.

- It supports 10 different languages.

- The initial top 10 Matching is free. The only paid part is an optional $3.75 trip kit for a single place (itinerary, 10 matched activities, checklist, PDF). It covers the Google Places API costs for venues and links, which seem oddly 'expensive'.

- Matching uses an LLM (currently xAI's Grok) to generate and reason about candidates, which get shaped into place cards, maps, short videos and activities.

One area I struggled with was how to group and refine the attribute selections. Higher slider levels reveal finer-grained choices and give that topic more weight. So if it matters a lot, you can really dial in what you're looking for. If it doesn't matter to you, you can skip entirely. If you see any that seem out of line, please point it out. It was a lot of work to make sense with the slider settings, and I'm not convinced it's dialed in.

Finally, if you're looking for something that doesn't have a selection, you can free-form a must-have before submitting.

Feedback welcome!

records.author: hermannbjorgvin
records.storyText:
A concept I wanted to share that is built on TailScale's Tailcat https://tailscale.com/tailcat

The inspiration is that I was thinking of ways to allow my users to be able to pool their machines easily without needing to set up SSH or a VPN.

How can you lower the barrier to entry without compromising on security.

The end result is you get a remote shell connection and a Tailcat tunnel that only requires your user to know how to use passkeys to verify their machines.

Any machine can join the pool without having connected to the others at any point before which is also a strength.

The primary weakness is that even though all the passkey assertion and encryption/decryption happens on the browser side you are still trusting a Cloudflare worker to store it. So I think this is more of a solution for things like Herdr, T3 code, etc etc where you want to connect machines in a pool. Each machine also has a small SQLite mail inbox for those purposes, you can queue messages that your machine will receive next time it is reachable.

records.storyText:
Lovable for Photo Editing. Think of it like having an AI agent use photoshop in front of you.
Just like with Lovable and vibe-coding, AI image editing is getting popular because it allows people to create beautiful edits of their photos without that specific domain expertise.
However, the problem with AI image editing approaches right now is that they regenerate the photo. This approach is prone to mistakes such as the image generation model adding or removing certain details, or introducing diffusion noise. And since it “edits” by regenerating the whole photo, it leaves little control for the user to tweak certain image editing parameters themselves. It is not a true edit.
PixlPal believes that AI should instead use deterministic tools (like in photoshop) to truly edit the images directly. So I created a custom Rust engine that exposes tools/APIs for an AI agent orchestrator to edit photos. The coolest part: I added a segmentation model that agents can call so it can select specific objects to apply specific transformations to as well.

records.storyText:
I built Crewplane because I wanted more control and flexibility over how my coding agents work together, and a way to trace what happened.

Workflow is defined in Markdown, and Crewplane runs the nodes defined in the workflow using native coding CLIs such as Codex and Claude Code. So the control is back to you: different workflows for different tasks with different models, what they depend on, and how they run (parallel or sequential or both). Every input, intermediate output, log, manifest, and final result is preserved on disk so you can trace a run after the fact.

Workflows can be reused and composed into larger pipelines, and interrupted workflows can be resumed. There is no vendor lock in, and it’s easy to adapt your workflows for various tasks - research, design, implementation, debugging, deployment, anything that works as structured procedures.

Give it a try and adapt your own workflows, there is a built-in Mock CLI so you can just try the workflow syntax and composition without worrying about costs (no model calls). Any feedback or suggestions would be greatly appreciated.
